key_facts: The claimant was convicted of two common assaults and sought an appeal by way of case stated under section 111 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980.
The Justices' Clerk accepted only one of eight drafted questions and did not refer the remaining questions of law to the lay magistrates.
The magistrates refused to state a case on the sole question put to them, treating the application as frivolous.
Judicial review was brought seeking an order requiring the magistrates to consider the omitted questions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of magistrates' refusal to state a case for the opinion of the High Court.
enrichment.outcome: Mandatory order requiring magistrates to consider two specified questions of law; no order as to inter partes costs, with legal aid taxation for the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: A Justices' Clerk may advise whether proposed questions raise points of law, but the decision whether to state a case rests with the magistrates and all properly formulated questions should be put to them; judicial review may require reconsideration unless the magistrates would inevitably have regarded further questions as frivolous.
legal_issues: Whether the Justices' Clerk could lawfully filter questions before referring an application to the magistrates
Whether magistrates' refusal to state a case on the only question referred was lawful
Which remaining questions raised arguable points of law on good character and evidential rulings
Whether costs should be ordered against the justices or Justices' Clerk

confidence.notes: Full administrative judgment with detailed procedural history and clear mandatory relief.

enrichment.short_title: Youth offender breach of detention and training order
key_facts: Andrew Stewart was convicted of failing to comply with a detention and training order by not reporting to the Youth Offending Team and not residing at a directed address.
Multiple concurrent DTOs were wrongly treated as separate offences in the memorandum of conviction although section 101(13) merged them into a single 18-month term.
The information charged duplicitous breaches but no prejudice arose and the appeal was largely academic after a later Crown Court sentence.
Proof of service of the section 103(7) supervision notice was inferred from attendance at the first supervision session and standard procedures.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Doncaster Youth Panel to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.ratio: Concurrent detention and training orders made on one occasion constitute a single term; proof of a section 103(7) notice may be inferred from conduct and standard practice; separate licence conditions may be duplicitous if charged together but that caused no injustice here.
legal_issues: Whether the information charged one offence or several
Whether direct proof of service of a section 103(7) notice was required
Admissibility of log-book evidence under section 24 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988
Whether residence and reporting breaches were separate offences

confidence.notes: Structured answers to six stated questions with clear statutory analysis.

enrichment.short_title: IAT must consider late expert country report
key_facts: Turkish Kurdish claimant's asylum appeal was dismissed by an adjudicator on credibility grounds.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal without considering an expert report by David McDowall commissioned after the adjudicator's decision.
The report was referred to in grounds of appeal and was capable of undermining several of the adjudicator's credibility findings.
Silber J refused permission on the papers but Keith J granted renewal on the expert-evidence ground.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; different tribunal member directed to reconsider leave in light of the McDowall report; costs awarded to the claimant.
enrichment.ratio: Where fresh expert evidence is referred to in an application for leave to appeal, the Tribunal must at least consider whether it is capable of affecting the real-prospect-of-success assessment; rule 18(11) does not prevent consideration of credible cogent evidence, and section 77 preserves a broad power to take relevant evidence into account.
legal_issues: Application of rule 18(11) to evidence not before the adjudicator
Whether good reasons were required for the late commissioning of expert evidence
Whether the McDowall report could undermine the adjudicator's credibility findings
Whether relief should be refused as a matter of discretion

linked_authorities.name: R v The Immigration Appeal Tribunal ex parte Aziz

confidence.notes: Detailed reasoning on rule 18(11), section 77 and the four credibility grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Reasonable notice to terminate exclusive agency
key_facts: Neptune terminated Alpha's long-standing exclusive UK agency for specialist valves on one month's notice in March 1998.
The judge found no oral contract variation in April 1996 over pricing and discount terms and that one month's notice was insufficient.
Damages of about £192,000 were awarded for eleven months' lost profit after allowing one month of notice given.
Neptune alleged an unfair trial because the deputy judge was robust with its witnesses, but the Court of Appeal rejected bias and unfairness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a Queen's Bench Division judgment on wrongful termination of an exclusive agency agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal largely dismissed; reasonable notice period varied from twelve months to four months with damages remitted for recalculation.
enrichment.ratio: Termination of an exclusive distributorship without repudiatory breach requires reasonable notice assessed at the time of termination by reference to relationship formality, turnover dependence and winding-down needs, not the manner or bad faith of termination; a full reinsurance clause was not in issue here but witness assessment and absence of agreed variation were upheld.
legal_issues: Whether the trial was unfair or showed apparent bias
Whether new pricing terms were orally agreed in April 1996
Whether the agency was terminable at will or only on reasonable notice
What period of reasonable notice applied and how damages should be calculated

enrichment.short_title: Pre-entry asylum controls at Prague Airport
key_facts: From July 2001 UK immigration officers operated pre-entry clearance at Prague Airport under agreement with the Czech Republic to deter Roma asylum seekers.
The European Roma Rights Centre and six Czech Roma challenged refusals of leave to enter on Convention, race discrimination and immigration rules grounds.
Burton J dismissed the claim and the Court of Appeal heard appeals on the Refugee Convention, immigration rules and Race Relations Act issues.
Intensive questioning of Roma was said to be justified because they were more likely to seek asylum covertly.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Administrative Court dismissing judicial review of extra-territorial immigration controls.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority; permission to appeal to the House of Lords granted; Laws LJ would have allowed the appeal on direct race discrimination.
enrichment.ratio: Operating immigration control abroad to refuse leave to enter before travel does not breach the Refugee Convention or require asylum to be treated as a permitted purpose under the rules where no valid claim exists; differential treatment of Roma based on greater likelihood of covert asylum claims is not direct racial discrimination because the reason is propensity to claim asylum, not race itself.
legal_issues: Whether extra-territorial pre-clearance breached the Refugee Convention
Whether refusing leave to Roma at Prague constituted direct discrimination under section 19B of the Race Relations Act 1976
Whether claiming asylum was a purpose covered by the immigration rules
Whether treaty ratification created enforceable legitimate expectations

linked_authorities.name: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Hoovespeed
R v Immigration Officer at Prague Airport, ex parte European Roma Rights Centre

confidence.notes: Very long judgment with split court on race discrimination; majority outcome and permission to HL are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Escaped horses: negligence but not keeper issue
key_facts: Brian Hole was seriously injured when his car collided with loose horses on the A352 early on 8 December 1997.
The horses were kept on Harry Ross-Skinner's land; a barbed wire fence had been cut and a gate from Top Park to Warmwell Lane was found open.
The trial judge found liability in negligence and under section 2(2) of the Animals Act 1971.
Strict liability under the Animals Act was accepted after Mirvahedy v Henley in the House of Lords; only the negligence finding was appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court finding of common law negligence; respondent did not oppose the appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on negligence; strict liability under the Animals Act remained accepted.
enrichment.ratio: General scruffiness of fencing on an estate is insufficient to establish negligence where the relevant fields were secure until a fence was cut and a gate opened by third parties; without evidence that the landowner's breach caused the escape, liability in negligence is not made out even where strict liability under the Animals Act may remain.
legal_issues: Whether the landowner breached a duty of care to maintain stock-proof fencing and gates
Whether any breach caused the horses to escape onto the highway
Whether general poor condition of fences elsewhere on the estate was enough to establish liability
Whether additional precautions against poachers were required

confidence.notes: Focused negligence appeal with clear causation reasoning and agreed strict-liability background.

enrichment.short_title: Croatian Serb returns test-case permission refused
key_facts: Five appeals substituted for the earlier S and Others test case considered whether ethnic Serbs could safely be returned to Croatia.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal held at a generic hearing that returned Serbs would not generally face persecution or Convention breaches, then rejected each appeal for lack of special circumstances.
Applicants challenged the 'factual precedent' approach and the Tribunal's treatment of expert and country evidence.
The appeals were conducted on a generic basis with extensive country materials rather than discrete individual arguments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from Immigration Appeal Tribunal determinations.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on all grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Where country-wide appeals are run generically and the Tribunal establishes background conditions for a nationality group, it may lawfully treat individual cases as asking whether exceptional circumstances take a claimant outside the general finding; expert evidence must be considered but a specialist tribunal's assessment of mass country evidence is not Wednesbury unreasonable merely because some expert views differ.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of a generic 'factual precedent' on conditions for returning Croatian Serbs
Whether the Tribunal failed to decide each appeal on its individual merits
Whether expert and country evidence was misunderstood or irrationally weighed
Article 14 read with Article 3 and exportability of Article 8 after Ullah

confidence.notes: Permission judgment with detailed treatment of generic appeals and expert evidence; Article 8 ground noted as blocked by Ullah.

key_facts: London market reinsurers covered 31.54% of Vitalicio's facultative reinsurance of an Atletico de Madrid policy for relegation and bonus risks.
The reinsurance slip described cover as indemnifying Atletico for net ascertained loss of television rights up to pts 2.9 billion.
The underlying Spanish policy indemnified Audiovisual for an agreed value of pts 2.9 billion if Atletico were relegated.
Atletico's first team was relegated in May 2000 and Vitalicio paid pts 2.7 billion to Audiovisual.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of reinsurers' claim for a declaration of non-liability and Vitalicio's counterclaim for payment.
enrichment.outcome: Reinsurers succeeded on misrepresentation and breach of warranty; counterclaim failed.
enrichment.ratio: A description of the insured interest on a facultative reinsurance slip may be a warranty going to the risk; describing the original policy as an indemnity for Atletico's ascertained loss when it was a valued policy for an agreed sum was material and induced underwriters to subscribe, and under Spanish law the clear agreed-value wording prevailed over later conduct.
legal_issues: Whether the full reinsurance clause imported a warranty matching the original policy terms
Whether the underlying policy was a valued or indemnity policy under Spanish law
Whether Atletico or Audiovisual was the insured under section one of the policy
Whether the misrepresentation was material and induced subscription to the reinsurance

enrichment.short_title: Initial notice invalid after work commenced
key_facts: Building works including a mezzanine floor at Kempston had substantially commenced before any building control notice was served.
An approved inspector served an Initial Notice on 4 July 2002 and a Plans Certificate on 18 July 2002.
Bedford Borough Council rejected the Plans Certificate because no valid Initial Notice was in force.
The approved inspector appealed under section 55 of the Building Act 1984.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates under section 55(1) of the Building Act 1984.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no valid Initial Notice existed and the Plans Certificate was lawfully rejected.
enrichment.ratio: An Initial Notice under section 47 must be given by a person intending to carry out work before substantial commencement; a notice served after unlawful commencement is not an Initial Notice at all, so the local authority need not reject it on prescribed grounds and may reject a Plans Certificate for want of a valid Initial Notice.
legal_issues: Whether an Initial Notice can be served after building work has substantially commenced
Effect of section 47(3) presumption of acceptance where no rejection occurs
Whether section 53(7) permits a fresh Initial Notice after partial completion
Whether regulation 21 regularisation was the required route after unauthorised commencement

confidence.notes: Agreed facts and detailed statutory construction with clear answers to stated questions.

enrichment.short_title: Section 17 costs and appeal route clarified

statutes_considered.title: Access to Justice Act 1999 (Commencement No 3, Transitional Provisions and Savings) Order 2000

key_facts: Former solicitors sought a section 17 determination that a legally aided client should pay over £36,000 in costs after a consent settlement.
Judge Brandt allowed an appeal and ordered a rehearing before another circuit judge, not an appeal-court rehearing under CPR 52.11.
Garland J wrongly treated Judge Thompson's decision as a second-tier appeal and declined jurisdiction.
Judge Thompson emphasised the client's conduct and history of negligence claims against solicitors but made no adequate findings on means.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on jurisdiction and, on its merits, against a section 17 costs assessment order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Garland J's jurisdictional decision set aside; section 17 order remitted for fresh assessment; costs orders varied.
enrichment.ratio: Where a circuit judge allows an appeal and orders a rehearing of the original application before another circuit judge, the subsequent challenge is a first-tier appeal not a CPR 52.11 rehearing; under section 17 the assisted party's means are a compelling circumstance and an order requiring payment of the full certified sum is not reasonable without explicit findings that he had sufficient resources.
legal_issues: Whether Judge Thompson's hearing was a first-instance rehearing or an appeal rehearing
Correct route of appeal from a section 17 costs determination
Proper approach to means and conduct under section 17 of the Legal Aid Act 1988
Effect of transitional Community Legal Service costs provisions

confidence.notes: Two-part judgment on jurisdiction and section 17 merits; transitional CLS points left open on remittal.
